prompt:
Write a Node.js ES module ini.mjs in the current folder (no npm packages) that exports one function, parse(text), which parses INI configuration text and returns a plain object.

Rules:
- The text is split into lines on \n or \r\n. Each line is trimmed of leading and trailing whitespace before it is looked at.
- Blank lines are ignored. Lines starting with ; or # are comments and are ignored.
- A line like [server] starts a section. The section name is whatever is between the brackets, trimmed (so "[ server ]" is the section "server"). The result holds each section as a nested plain object: { server: { ... } }. A section with no keys still appears as an empty object. The same section name appearing twice is merged into one object.
- Any other line must be a key and value separated by the FIRST = sign: "key = value". Key and value are both trimmed. Everything after the first = belongs to the value, including further = signs, ; and # characters (there are no inline comments, so "url = http://x/?a=1 ; not a comment" has the value "http://x/?a=1 ; not a comment"). An empty value is allowed and gives the empty string.
- If the trimmed value both starts and ends with a double quote and has at least two characters, the quotes are removed and the text between them is used exactly as written, so spaces inside the quotes are kept: name = "  padded  " gives "  padded  ".
- All values are strings. Nothing is converted to numbers or booleans.
- Keys that appear before any section header go directly on the top level object.
- If the same key appears twice in the same place, the later value wins.
- A line that is not a comment, not a section header and has no = sign throws an Error with the message `Invalid line N: <the trimmed line>` where N is the 1 based line number counting every line of the text, including blank ones. A line that starts with [ but does not end with ] throws the same kind of error. A line with an empty key (such as "= value") also throws that error. An empty section name "[]" throws it too.

Example:
parse("name = demo\n; note\n[server]\nhost = localhost\nport = 8080\n") returns { name: "demo", server: { host: "localhost", port: "8080" } }.
